items.author: 1axbtwoq239im3vds5bhycqyj7inh0vraysn9v@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Shortly after the election, I came to you with a bold prediction: once all the ballots were counted and the results certified, Democrats would hold 56 Senate seats. I can now report that my prediction came true.

Throughout the post-election period, I have worn two hats. I am the chairman of Elias Law Group, the law firm that helped secure the final victories. I am also the founder of Democracy Docket, an outlet that had reporters on the ground.

During that time, Democracy Docket provided you with in-depth reporting, analysis and commentary on what was happening and what to expect next. There was no hedging, no false equivalence and no both-sides journalism.

When Mississippi’s secretary of state tried to blame third-party vendors for high rates of ballots flagged for further review, rather than counted outright, Democracy Docket covered it. When the Department of Justice threatened, and then abandoned, a legal effort to block Alaska’s certification, Democracy Docket cut through the spin and told you what was really at stake.

Throughout it all, I offered my analysis in writing and on video podcasts. Thanks to support from its premium members, Democracy Docket dropped its paywall from Election Day until the Alaska race was called.

During that period, one of the most visited parts of the Democracy Docket website was its live blog, which kept you updated on the remaining races to be called. It featured a mix of short and long written pieces, along with video reports from the states.

Democracy Docket could provide this feature for free because it built its own technology platform. That may seem minor, but think about what it meant in practice.

If we had relied on a corporate platform that decided, under political pressure, to restrict or remove us, you could have lost access to that live blog in the middle of the Alaska fight, precisely when accurate information mattered most.

That is why Democracy Docket built its own custom technology stack: to ensure it is never beholden to venture capital firms, tech CEOs or corporations whose interests and alliances shift with the wind. Honestly, this makes operating Democracy Docket harder, more expensive and often a headache.

But managing our own platform is another way we ensure Democracy Docket stays fiercely independent and unapologetically pro-democracy. It makes it far harder for any one company to be pressured by Donald Trump into cutting us off, and far harder for any one vendor to cripple us.

There are other benefits as well.

It is never sold or traded, and you won’t receive emails urging you to sign up for some other site or product.

There are no Nazis on Democracy Docket, no right-wing propaganda and no one promoting crypto schemes.

, our subscribers and members, including by hosting a live blog in the middle of a critical election.

Across the country, we’ve watched media owners and executives curry favor with Trump, trading tough coverage for access or bowing to the fear of lawsuits, investigations and prosecution. Democracy Docket is built to withstand those pressures.

Democracy Docket is powered by premium members who pay $120 a year, just $10 a month, for access to all of its content. It simply cannot do its work without them. If you are able, please consider joining the more than 70,000 members who make this work possible.

We have fought long and hard for this victory, but this is not the end of the road. Donald Trump is still in the White House. The weaponization of government against Trump’s political opponents is escalating.

Democracy Docket will be there every step of the way. I am proud to have you on our team.

What does it take to sustain a movement for nearly 80 years?

Persistence. The willingness to keep doing the work, generation after generation, as the challenges change and the stakes evolve.

Today, Americans United celebrates 79 years of doing exactly that. Over nearly eight decades, AU has helped end government-sponsored prayer and Bible reading in public schools, challenged religious discrimination, defended LGBTQ+ equality and reproductive freedom, and brought countless cases protecting the separation of church and state.

We also have some incredible news to share with you: In a win for religious freedom and church-state separation, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction yesterday in our lawsuit, blocking U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins from continuing to proselytize 100,000 USDA employees. 

This crucial decision sends a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach, hold government-sponsored prayer services during work time, and broadcast Christian Nationalism over official communication channels.

This important win – and celebrating another year of Americans United – is what persistence looks like to me. It’s not simply staying in the work, but building the people and institutions that will sustain it for generations to come.

Friend, help us carry this work forward.

items.title: Big Law sold out to save itself
items.author: 1axcjxcfssq191s8m1y2gqeprvibr72b7trmjn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
When Donald Trump’s executive orders and Department of Justice lawsuits attacked voting and elections, Big Law was nowhere to be found. Yet when Trump needed free legal services, at least one law firm, Kirkland & Ellis, was there to help.

In April 2025, to avoid a punishing executive order, Kirkland agreed to provide $125 million in free legal work for causes the White House supported. It was one of nine Big Law firms that together pledged $940 million under similar deals.

Now we know what some of that work looked like.

According to news reports, Kirkland provided nearly $12 million in free legal services, totaling more than 6,400 hours, to agencies including the Commerce and Defense Departments. In addition, according to MSNOW, the firm “also estimated that it has done $18.7 million in free legal work for outside clients in the causes Trump listed in the Truth Social post announcing the deal.”

Importantly, Kirkland is only the first of the nine firms to provide this information to Democratic members of the House and Senate, who are preparing to conduct oversight on the issue. We have not yet heard from Paul Weiss, which led Big Law’s capitulation to Trump, or from the other firms that seemed eager to get in on the action.

Kirkland wants us to believe it was the victim of a threat.

items.title: How homelessness and racism intersect.
items.author: SRS0=kL4K=JH=mail70.suw17.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295061-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Homelessness Funding Is on the Line. Here’s How to Protect It.

Today, the National Alliance to End Homelessness is leading a national day of action to protect federal homelessness funding (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Advocates are asking Congress to add a few lines to its next spending bill that would require the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to renew every Continuum of Care project expiring this fiscal year for 12 months, without a new competition (National Low Income Housing Coalition).

The Continuum of Care program is the largest federal source of money for local homelessness work. It pays for programs like permanent supportive housing, where people get a stable home along with services like health care and job support (National Low Income Housing Coalition), and transitional housing, which gives people a safe place to stay while they look for a permanent home (National Association of Counties).

The Trump administration has spent the past year trying to limit spending on homelessness. In July 2025, the president signed an executive order directing agencies to end support for Housing First policies, which give people a permanent home quickly without first requiring sobriety, treatment or a job (The White House). But Housing First has been federal policy under presidents of both parties since 2003 (Associated Press), and it has proven to be the most effective way to rehouse people (National Alliance to End Homelessness).

HUD then wrote new rules for this year’s Continuum of Care grants that put the president’s order into practice. In August, a federal judge ruled that those rules were unlawful. HUD had set aside $1.3 billion of this year’s funding for new transitional housing and service-only projects, a change that would have cut money from many programs already keeping people housed (National Association of Counties). The judge also struck down rules that required programs to follow the president’s executive orders and restricted diversity efforts. But in September, an appeals court let HUD move forward while it considers the case. Under HUD’s plan, only 60 percent of funding would be protected for renewals, down from nearly 90 percent. Advocates estimate that 97,000 people who were once unhoused could lose their housing as a result (National Low Income Housing Coalition).

The delays are already hurting people. In Los Angeles, providers that serve domestic violence survivors and unhoused people have cut staff and drained their reserves while HUD held up their grants (LAist). As of September, more than 1,300 renewal grant agreements across the country, about one in five, had not been fully executed. “If HUD doesn’t start to reimburse agencies quickly … we’re going to see more suffering on the street,” said Myong Kim of the Downtown Women’s Center in Los Angeles.

The people impacted by these funding cuts are disproportionately people of color. Black people are 14 percent of the U.S. population but 33 percent of people experiencing homelessness. Latino people make up 27.5 percent of the unhoused population, and Native and Pacific Islander people are also overrepresented. These numbers reflect generations of policy, from redlining to exclusionary zoning to landlords and lenders who still screen people out by eviction records and criminal background (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Today, Black renters are 28 percent of renters in the places Eviction Lab tracks, but 39 percent of the people facing eviction (Eviction Lab).

While funding for housing is under attack, more places are choosing punishment instead. Since the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in Grants Pass v. Johnson, more than 350 cities and 14 states have adopted tougher laws on street homelessness (Stateline). In 2022, we spoke with Jamaal of ACT UP Philadelphia about the violence of encampment sweeps (Anti-Racism Daily). “Philly says all the time, ‘We can’t afford to house people, the housing is too expensive,’ but every time we turn around, they increase funding to the police,” he told us. I think about that line a lot, because it’s still true in so many cities.

To be clear, renewing these grants won’t end homelessness on its own. We still need far more affordable homes, higher wages and an end to policies that punish people for being poor. But keeping existing programs running is the least Congress can do, and it’s within reach this month. If you have five minutes today, I encourage you to send that email. For many families, these few lines in a spending bill could decide whether they stay housed this winter.

items.title: Trump lost the race he bet everything on
items.author: 1axbqhwmo0qcdwqoqfjj3xipe99odyaoflv15f@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Last night, Mary Peltola officially won Alaska’s Senate race. The Division of Elections updated its results to show she held an outright majority. The outcome is undeniable.

With Peltola’s victory, Donald Trump lost the one fight he cared about most.

For months, Trump obsessed over this race. Even as he watched Republicans get swept from coast to coast, his focus stayed fixed on Alaska.

Weighed down by his historic unpopularity, his party lost Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and South Carolina. Even Mississippi.

State after state, as the election returns came in, Trump could do nothing to stop the bleeding.

Yet, as his party imploded, Trump seethed and raged about Sen. Dan Sullivan’s looming defeat in Alaska.

He spread misinformation about how Alaskans vote. He lied about the results, insisting that votes cast for a different candidate belonged to the incumbent.

He ordered his Justice Department to sue to block certification. When my law firm beat back that lawsuit, the DOJ came after me personally. Trump went on national television and said I should go to jail.

None of these attacks changed the vote count. With each new batch of ballots, Peltola’s lead grew.

Last night, the dam broke.

Peltola now leads by 12,458 votes. More importantly, she has won more than half of all the votes cast in the race.

There will be no ranked-choice tabulation, and no room for conspiracy theories about whose votes “really” belonged to whom.

And with that, Trump’s lies collapse once and for all.

Sullivan’s campaign says he won’t concede until the results are certified. The campaign insists it will “let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.”

Fortunately, election results are stubborn. The numbers are what they are. They do not require a concession to be accurate. They do not care about the losing candidate’s feelings or his stage of grief.

Despite all of Trump’s bluster, Mary Peltola will be the next senator from Alaska. A Yup’ik Alaskan and former congresswoman, she made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, with the rest of the newly elected class.

She will join a radically changed Congress. In the House, Democrats will hold a historic 260-seat majority. But it is the 56 seats in the Senate that have truly upended Trump’s agenda.

With margins like these, Trump will no longer be able to confirm his cronies and sycophants. His judicial nominees will languish. Any Supreme Court vacancy will remain unfilled.

With 56 seats, Democrats won’t just control the Senate for the next two years. They are almost certain to hold the majority for the next four. And if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028, a Democratic Senate will be ready to fill every vacancy Trump leaves behind.

Trump will fare no better with his legislative agenda. Democrats in Congress will decide which bills reach his desk. Trump will be reduced to nothing more than a signature — signing or vetoing the bills placed before him.

The question remains: Why Alaska? Of all the defeats and humiliations Trump suffered this year, why did Dan Sullivan’s loss sting the most?

Trump will say it’s because he believes Democrats cheated. But Trump has never cared about cheating.

In 2020, he told Georgia’s secretary of state to “find” 11,780 votes that did not exist. In September, he stood before the Republican convention in Dallas and instructed his supporters to “cheat like hell” in this year’s elections. 

In any event, Trump’s lies are no longer sustainable. We now know that Peltola won an outright majority. No theory about confused voters or a second Dan Sullivan can explain away a candidate who won more votes than everyone else combined.

The simplest answer is the most likely. Trump’s focus on Alaska is the fixation of an elderly man whose mental faculties are declining.

It is the same fixation that has caused him to dedicate his presidency to a White House ballroom, a public golf course in Washington, D.C., and a triumphal arch. All while his party burned.

Whatever the reason, Trump bet everything on Alaska, and he lost. For the rest of us, Peltola’s victory is cause for celebration. Let’s take a moment to enjoy it.

items.title: Trump says I should go to jail
items.author: 1axbtgroo9jlo0q00k7zsvogooq1j45ibhesbn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
The United States is in the midst of a constitutional crisis. I do not make this claim lightly or with any intended hyperbole. I am saying it now because too few are willing to speak out. If we fail to recognize it for what it is, it will only get worse.

Despite what we want to believe about what is “normal,” for the last decade, United States elections have been held hostage. We live under threat that one major party will not accept the results.

The president uses his power to target vote counting and certification. He deploys federal prosecutors to intimidate opposition figures.

If this were another country, would we not agree that it faces a constitutional crisis? Would we say the crisis is over because the sitting president and his party failed in their efforts to subvert the midterm elections?

I understand that mine is not a popular opinion.

Those on the right want to act as if Donald Trump’s actions have been justified all along. Many on the left want to celebrate the midterms as if the threat has been defeated. Much of the legacy media sees its role as questioning whether the crisis ever existed at all.

To be clear, litigating election rules and contesting election results does not by itself create a constitutional crisis.

A constitutional crisis occurs when those who hold power systematically weaponize the machinery of government against the very institutions the Constitution relies on to check that power. At a minimum, those checks include free and fair elections, equal treatment under the law and respect for democratic outcomes.

This is an intentionally narrow definition. Even after Jan. 6, 2021, I did not view the 2020 election as a crisis of constitutional dimensions.

As despicable as his actions were, Trump was acting largely as a defeated candidate. The scores of lawsuits filed by him and his allies relied on private resources. When he pressed the Department of Justice to intervene, its leadership refused.

In the end, the federal government did not become an instrument for altering the results. Trump considered a draft executive order in December 2020 that would have directed the Pentagon to seize voting machines, but he ultimately did not sign it.

The threats to the 2026 midterms were far more serious, because this time the government itself was the instrument.

It was the DOJ, not GOP campaigns, that tried to coerce states to turn over their sensitive voter data. It was by executive orders that Trump tried to tamper with state voting laws and weaponize the U.S. Postal Service. It was at the president’s direction that the DOJ tried to block the certification of a Democrat in the Alaska Senate race.

Most troubling has been the increased abuse of criminal law to threaten election officials and political opponents. These tactics began before the election. It was the FBI, under Kash Patel, that seized Fulton County, Georgia’s 2020 ballots and election records in January 2026.

But they have continued and escalated ever since.

I know this firsthand. I have spent my career representing Democrats in election litigation. That work has resulted in handing scores of defeats to Trump and Republicans in cases involving close elections.

In 2020, I helped lead the litigation to defeat Trump and his allies more than 60 times. In the run-up to this election, my law firm defeated Trump’s DOJ more than 30 times in court.

Only days before Election Day, it was revealed that Trump’s DOJ considered me a target of a criminal probe involving the Alaska Senate race. That designation came notwithstanding the U.S. Attorney saying that he wasn’t certain if there was any crime committed by anyone.

That did not matter to Trump. In the days that followed, the president repeatedly said on national television and on social media that I should go to jail.

After initially saying he would accept the results, Trump backtracked and suggested they were rigged.

When congressional Democrats made clear they would conduct oversight, Trump announced he was ordering the Justice Department to look into it. His White House counsel then warned that their investigative plans could cross into criminal behavior.

Critics of my argument will point out that no 2026 ballots were seized, no federal law enforcement appeared at the polls and Democrats won resounding victories. They will note that those results are being certified at the state level, and there is no indication that the peaceful transfer of power in Congress on Jan. 3, 2027, will not take place.

Above all, they will point out that the courts largely reined in the president’s actions and that their orders were followed.

Such a myopic view confuses Trump’s actions with the election results. Voters can overcome an abuse of power, but that does not make it any less an abuse.

With the help of the courts, voters may have defeated the attacks on our elections, but that does not diminish the attacks’ significance. And these claims ignore what is continuing to happen.

A bank teller who foils a robbery is still the victim of a crime. And if more robberies continue to occur at other banks, the spree has not ended.

The question is not whether Trump’s efforts succeeded. It is whether the executive branch went along with them and continues to do so.

Some pundits will say that I am raising a false alarm, that all of this shows how strong our elections are and that the system of protecting against government abuses has worked. But this misses the point.

Courts are imperfect protectors of democracy. They can block only what has already been attempted, and only after someone sues. A system that survives only by winning dozens of emergency lawsuits or by the falsely accused being exonerated at trial is neither healthy nor sustainable.

Now that voters have handed Congress to the Democrats, we are seeing an escalation of, not a retreat from, Trump’s attacks on the Constitution. His administration is systematically targeting congressional oversight.

Perhaps Democratic officials will remain strong in the face of these threats. Will the same be true of the staff and witnesses who make oversight possible?

I have grown accustomed to being targeted by Trump. But how many other lawyers will shy away from taking on the administration if the threat of prosecution is the cost of doing the work?

If all of this were happening in another country, we would know what to call it. A country whose leader turned the full force of the government he controls against its own elections, his political opponents and congressional leaders would not be considered a normal democracy.

It would be described as a democracy in crisis. If it had a robust constitution, it would be called a constitutional crisis. We should be willing to say the same about our own.

Calling this crisis what it is will allow us to do something about it. It will empower the courts to protect democracy. It will encourage Congress to assert its power, conduct oversight over the administration and enact needed reforms.

Most importantly, recognizing that we are in a constitutional crisis will allow us to fully and finally commit to defeating the threat Trump has posed over the last decade, and the threat his movement poses in the years ahead.

items.author: SRS0=0iS3=JE=mail70.suw17.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295050-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Transgender Awareness Week is held every November as a nationwide initiative to raise awareness about the issues that trans communities face (GLAAD). The week leads up to Transgender Day of Remembrance on Nov. 20. The event started in 1999 to honor Rita Hester, a Black trans woman killed the year before, and all those who have lost their lives to anti-trans violence (GLAAD). You can read more about Transgender Day of Remembrance in our issue of 28 Days of Black History, published last February.

This year's observances come at a pivotal time in our fight for trans rights. We just ended the midterm elections, where conservative political leaders and their supporters spent an estimated $183 million on trans-focused ads, mostly attacking Democrats who support trans people (Prism). And it wasn't only Republicans. Democrats in at least 17 states took public anti-trans positions, too (Prism).

We know that strategy mostly failed. Most of the Democrats targeted by those ads won, including Texas' James Talarico, Ohio's Sherrod Brown and Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed (Prism). In an October poll, voters from both parties ranked trans issues last out of 20, far behind inflation, housing and health care. Even Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the ads were "not the issue motivating voters" (Prism).

But the ads added to the growing anti-trans sentiment that the Trump administration has pushed over the past couple of years. And that rhetoric has been paired with real efforts to limit trans people's rights. In 2026 alone, lawmakers introduced 840 anti-trans bills across 43 states and Congress, and 63 have passed so far (Trans Legislation Tracker). Most of these bills target health care and schools, the places where trans youth need the most support.

During the midterm election, voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington approved bans on trans girls playing on girls' school sports teams (Prism). Washington's Initiative 638 goes further, requiring girls to "verify" their sex in a health exam before they can play. Groups have already sued to stop it from taking effect.

And trans communities feel the impact. In a national survey, 90% of LGBTQ+ young people said recent anti-LGBTQ+ laws, policies and debates caused them stress or anxiety (The Trevor Project). Four in 10 trans and nonbinary young people seriously considered suicide in the past year. And 44% of LGBTQ+ young people who wanted mental health care weren't able to get it (The Trevor Project).

Trans people – particularly trans people of color – are most vulnerable to racism, sexism and transphobia. When we center their needs in our advocacy efforts, we lift the tide for all people. Consider how our anti-trans rhetoric now exposes both cis and trans girls to uncomfortable questions about their bodies, or how efforts to stymie access to gender-affirming care make it harder for cis and trans people to get the medical support they need.

items.title: I’m watching Alaska closely
items.author: 1axbu1qhql2swxa1lge2scp6h8nkgbk7gswfr3@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Whoever said everything is bigger in Texas hasn’t been to Alaska. The Last Frontier is bigger than Texas, California and Montana combined.

The largest national park in the country is in Alaska. Its name is one of my favorites: Wrangell–St. Elias.

But Alaska’s size is more than a point of pride. It also makes voting there remarkably hard. The state’s beautiful but isolated landscape creates complications for voters, and dozens of polling places are in towns without road access.

Voting by mail isn’t simple either, as extreme weather can cause days-long delays. In some remote villages, polling places without election workers fail to open at all.

Though the networks still haven’t called Alaska’s Senate race, it is clear that Mary Peltola is poised to win and become the 56th member of the Senate Democratic caucus come January.

Peltola’s likely victory and its close margin prove two truths. First, every vote matters, and the fight to ensure every vote is counted is essential to democracy. Second, Democrats can win anywhere they have the candidates and resources to compete.

Sadly, Alaska’s elections have also been the target of one of Donald Trump’s fiercest attacks, and he is showing no signs of letting up.

Less than two weeks before Election Day, Trump’s Department of Justice sued to block Alaska from certifying Peltola as the winner if she defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. My firm, Elias Law Group, intervened on behalf of the Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to fight back.

We won: two days before the election, a federal judge dismissed the case. The DOJ has appealed but seems in a hurry to further litigate their defeat.

Then the Trump DOJ launched criminal investigations without being able to confirm that any crime had been committed. In the days before the election, the DOJ leaked that I was among its targets.

Trump has targeted me before. He hates me because I fight and win.

After the 2020 election, I helped lead the legal effort that defeated him and his allies more than 60 times. My firm just helped Scott Colom unseat Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and win Mississippi’s U.S. Senate race. Now we are fighting in Alaska.

I have no doubt that Trump’s hatred of me is only growing. I wear his scorn as a badge of honor.

But even the best legal work won’t protect democracy from Trump’s lies and smears. That requires pro-democracy platforms and outlets that tell the truth without fear or compromise.

Democracy Docket covered the count in Mississippi from start to finish, and now its team is on the ground in Alaska. The team is watching and reporting closely, bringing readers daily updates and insights as the race unfolds.

I created Democracy Docket for exactly this kind of moment. While other outlets offer horse-race coverage and both-sides analysis, Democracy Docket covers free and fair elections every day of the year through an uncompromisingly pro-democracy lens.

We shine a light on the voting rights fights the national spotlight misses. It breaks down court cases months before Election Day and follows stories years before they reach the front pages of legacy media.

After much discussion, Democracy Docket has decided to keep its paywall down, as it has been since Election Day, until the Alaska race is called. This was not an easy decision.

But as Trump and the GOP continue to spread lies about this election, the stakes are too high to keep anything behind a paywall.

Members keep Democracy Docket’s website and podcasts free for everyone and make it possible to keep the paywall down as the fight for Alaska continues. They also get my written analysis: what’s happening in the courts, what each ruling means for the next election, and where the fight is headed before anyone else is talking about it.

If you’ve been reading my analysis since the paywall came down on Election Day, you already know what you’d be missing.

If you can’t upgrade right now, I understand. As always, thank you for being a subscriber and reader. But if you do, I would deeply appreciate it.

All eyes are on Alaska today, but at Democracy Docket, we will keep our eyes trained on the Last Frontier every day.

The battle for free and fair elections does not end when the networks make their call. It lives on as long as we are willing to fight.

items.title: Why is no one talking about this?
items.author: 1axbu94jjhaneq2wl1qmrqxrtbrs0tar9a47fn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Earlier this week, amid all the excitement in Mississippi and uncertainty in Alaska, a federal judge quietly closed the book on the Department of Justice’s lawsuit against California. The DOJ had sued to force the state to set aside more than 20,000 ballots it did not want counted.

After aggressively litigating the case all the way to the Supreme Court, and losing at every level, the DOJ asked the court to dismiss its own lawsuit. The court obliged.

Only two weeks ago, the specter of the DOJ prosecuting election officials for counting ballots hung over the Golden State and elections nationwide. We watched as the Trump administration escalated its lies and demands. We worried that this case might be a prelude to seizing ballots.

The order closing the case was a simple one page. But in it, U.S. District Judge David O. Carter offered one last statement explaining what had been at stake:

“This lawsuit attempted to disrupt an ongoing election and create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers alike. The right to vote is sacred. So, too, is trust in our democracy.”

These words echo what conservative Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas wrote six years ago when he sternly rejected the Trump campaign’s challenge to the 2020 presidential election in Pennsylvania:

“Free, fair elections are the lifeblood of our democracy. Charges of unfairness are serious. But calling an election unfair does not make it so. Charges require specific allegations and then proof. We have neither here.”

The parallels between November 2020 and today are striking. In both instances, Trump’s party lost hotly contested elections. Both involved litigation Trump instigated to try to change the outcome. And both then and now, the courts soundly rejected his outrageous claims.

Beneath those similarities, however, lie disturbing differences.

The Pennsylvania case in 2020 was litigated by a bumbling Rudy Giuliani on behalf of the Trump campaign. It was the dying gasp of a losing campaign.

The California case, by contrast, was filed by the Department of Justice. It was not born of desperation; it was part of a larger, premeditated attack on free and fair elections.

And while the Pennsylvania lawsuit sought to throw out lawful votes, the California case went further. It was paired with threats to investigate and prosecute state and local election officials.

Perhaps most importantly, the dismissal of the Pennsylvania case was celebrated in the national media as a triumph of democracy over efforts to discredit free and fair elections. The dismissal of the California case this week barely registered outside a handful of outlets.

Over the last two years, there have been many instances of Trump’s aberrant and destructive behavior. None has done more damage to the nation’s identity than his ceaseless attacks on our elections.

But worse than Trump’s conduct is the way it has been normalized in places that once would have found it outrageous and worthy of unsparing condemnation.

If a federal judge can remain judicious while saying the DOJ’s lawsuit “attempted to disrupt an ongoing election,” why can’t the legacy media use similarly direct language? If a court is willing to say the DOJ’s intent was to “create confusion and uncertainty for voters and election workers,” why can’t our civic leaders say the same?

After the 2020 election, for a brief time at least, this was not a problem. After Jan. 6, 2021, the condemnation of Trump was forceful and uncompromising.

He was impeached, and a bipartisan majority of the Senate voted to convict him. Media outlets across the spectrum spoke in clear moral terms. Business leaders pledged to support democracy.

Yet today, as Democrats celebrate their victories and the GOP nurses its wounds, there is near silence about Trump’s assault on voting and elections. It is as if it were a passing phase, a remnant of the pre-election period that we can now forget.

This was the mistake many made after Trump left office the first time. We thought he was gone and his movement discredited. The initial shock and outrage over his behavior wore off. Corporate pledges quietly lapsed. Polite society moved on.

How many more elections must we endure in which the threats reach critical levels? How many more times can we ask lawyers and the courts to bail us out?

In the coming weeks, Democrats will take power in Congress and in states around the country. They must address the threats we have endured for nearly a decade under Trump and the MAGA Republicans.

That means enacting strong new voting laws, protecting voters and election officials from intimidation, and conducting oversight over the executive branch’s unlawful actions.

We as citizens must do our part as well.

That means calling and writing our representatives and demanding that they use every tool available to them. It means showing up when our legislatures debate election laws. And it means standing up, speaking out and working to defeat Trumpism as an ideology.

I understand that there are many other important issues facing our country, from the cost of living to health care. But unless we fix our democracy, none of those other problems will be solved.

Over the next few months, I plan to make this a central theme of my writing and advocacy. I hope you will join me. Subscribe to Democracy Docket to follow along.

items.title: Scott Colom prevailed
items.author: delivery_20261112061301.48379211.277@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
The blue tsunami hit over a week ago, and it’s still making waves for Democrats. We’re looking at you Mississippi—one of the reddest states in the country was finally called for Democrat Scott Colom. He will be the first elected Black senator for the state in over 150 years, unseating Republican incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. Colom’s win came down to just a few thousand votes, and each side had lawyered up in anticipation of an ugly legal battle. The entire process has highlighted just how archaic Mississippi’s voting system is, even as—this time—democracy seems to have prevailed.

On Wednesday evening, Mississippi’s senate race was called for Colom, who ended up carrying the state by about 4,600 votes over Hyde-Smith. Now, election officials will finalize remaining affidavit ballots, including ones for voters who had their registrations incorrectly marked inactive after a massive purge of Mississippi’s voter rolls ahead of this year’s midterm elections. Come Friday, county election commissioners for all of Mississippi’s 82 counties have to submit their certified election results to the secretary of state’s office. Then, on December 3, Secretary of State Michael Watson is scheduled to declare the statewide general election results.

The Colom and Hyde-Smith campaigns have indicated they are preparing for potential legal action, with both sides deploying small armies of attorneys and observers to monitor the ballot counting process. Challenging whether certain ballots should be counted is one of the only ways candidates can contest the outcome of a federal Senate race in Mississippi, as it is the only state in the country that does not have a law in place for automatic vote recounts in close races. The state also does not have a law in place mandating runoff elections. That means that Colom and Hyde-Smith must wait until final results of their election are announced before they can file a lawsuit (with the potential to result in a recount), which could happen any time after Friday’s deadline. 

Two days after Election Day, Hyde-Smith’s campaign sent a letter to each county election commissioner and circuit clerk for all 82 Mississippi counties demanding they separate all affidavit ballots from regular and absentee ballots. Affidavit ballots are generally used when a voter does not have their ID or was previously marked as inactive, as was the case for upward of 200,000 Mississippi voters after Watson partnered with credit agency Experian to purge the state’s voter rolls. In order to validate an affidavit ballot, voters have to physically go to their circuit clerk’s office and present their ID within five business days of filing that affidavit ballot in order for it to be counted.

This is a move straight out of the Trump administration’s playbook, as the Justice Department in October similarly demanded California election officials separate mail ballots for about 20,000 voters it claimed it suspected were noncitizens trying to vote. A federal judge ruled against the DOJ, writing that separating ballots would “risk disenfranchising an untold number of voters” and “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway” and  “create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike.”

Nevertheless, Hyde-Smith’s team insisted that separating affidavit ballots is required by Mississippi law and federal law, so that each one “can be verified.” That very same day, Colom’s campaign fired off their own letter to Mississippi’s election officials acknowledging Hyde-Smith’s demands and warning that if they depart from ordinary election procedures, they “will violate Mississippi voters’ rights and Mississippi election law.” So, who’s right here?

Well, the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled on this issue back in 1975 in Clark v. Rankin County Democratic Executive Com.and concluded that separating certain ballots is unlawful because it undermines “the secrecy of a voter’s ballot.” Colom’s campaign also noted that the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in asserted that the “arbitrary and disparate treatment of voters in its different counties” amounts to “a constitutional violation” of the equal protection clause of the 14th Amendment. 

It’s also worth noting that in the event that Hyde-Smith or Colom is successful in forcing a recount through filing a lawsuit, these types of procedures “ change the results of elections,” as Derek Muller, Notre Dame law professor, noted on the Election Law Blog. So far, the slow dribble of counting affidavit and mail ballots has favored Colom, something he predicted at the outset of Election Day. “The affidavit [ballots] always move in the Democrats favor in Mississippi. If you look at the ballots that are left, it’s going in our favor,” Colom told reporters. 

Mississippi was not on Democrats’ wish list heading into the midterm elections, relegated as a state that was impossible to flip from Republicans, something Colom argued hurts many Southern Democrats. But as his campaign catapulted to the national stage on Election Day and has since captivated the national news media, Mississippi’s Senate race also sheds light on how the state has gotten away with suppressing voting rights for decades. It's one of three states that does not offer early voting, while it requires an excuse to vote by mail. The state also strips individuals convicted of certain felonies of their right to vote. In this race alone, 24 percent of affidavit ballots were rejected for issues such as having an incorrect county registration or the person voting at the incorrect precinct. The rejections appear to have been much more severe in deeply blue counties.

Meanwhile, Mississippi is home to the highest share of Black voters, who account for nearly 40 percent of the state’s population, yet lawmakers have ensured there is only Black-majority district in the entire state. Even that may go away soon, as state Republicans considered redistricting, now a perfectly legal endeavor thanks to the Supreme Court’s decision. However, on Nov. 3, Mississippi voters showed up and showed out in numbers that are proving to be insurmountable, in spite of all the barriers they face.

There is good reason to feel encouraged right now. Across the country, we have been reminded that progress is possible and the future is still ours to shape.

items.title: The Word of the Day: Accountability
items.author: bounce_a1d1deb5-a5de-f111-91f0-000d3a18e244_prod@bounce.myngp.com
items.content:
Sesame Street once featured a regular segment, , in which Muppet characters and a celebrity guest explained a specific vocabulary word. Their choices evoke nostalgia for words that today are often derided as weakness, for example, diversity, belonging, fairness, and kindness. 

were applied to this post-election climate, two would dominate: Accountability and Affordability. Which should Congress be working to solve? But this is not a binary choice. If that Sesame Street segment existed today, perhaps the wisdom of Big Bird and Elmo could break through the cacophony to explain how interdependent these concepts actually are.

Affordability is built on the rule of law and requires a system of commerce that is fair, predictable, and offers a level playing field for all. If the rules are changed to allow those in power to dole out favors to their friends and supporters while punishing their enemies, affordability for all becomes unachievable.

Accountability provides the foundation for affordability. Just as government leaders are accountable to voters, government lawyers are accountable to the Constitution and to rules of professional conduct, the oath they swore when they became lawyers, and the rules of a fair justice system. If government lawyers are dishonest or mislead the court, fail to adhere to the rules that govern our profession, or attack judges personally for decisions they do not agree with, then the public itself is harmed.

LDAD has helped pioneer the notion that lawyers in the public sphere must be held accountable when they undermine a free and fair election or ignore rules that apply to government agencies and their leaders.This week, LDAD and 53 scholars and retired judges filed an against three senior Department of Justice officials: Harmeet Dhillon, the former Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; Robert Keenan, Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division; and Eric Neff, Acting Chief of the Voting Section.

The complaint alleges that Ms. Dhillon, Mr. Keenan, and Mr. Neff violated their professional and ethical obligations by pursuing lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia, jurisdictions that refused to provide the Department of Justice with unredacted voter records containing millions of Americans' sensitive personal information, including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, addresses, and voting histories, and continued to pursue claims that courts repeatedly rejected as legally unsupported. As of October 23, 2026, DOJ had lost all 27 cases in which courts issued a ruling, as well as the first appellate decision addressing the DOJ’s demands for this voter information. Yet DOJ continued to pursue the same baseless legal theories rejected by the courts.

LDAD also recently sought accountability by filing an against Hugh Evans, a member of the Alabama bar who serves as a special agent of the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The complaint concerns the sworn affidavit Mr. Evans submitted to a U.S. Magistrate Judge in January 2026 to obtain a search warrant for 2020 election records held by Fulton County, Georgia. The FBI executed that warrant on January 28, 2026, seizing more than 650 boxes of ballots and other election materials. The complaint alleges that the affidavit withheld from the court material information: that Georgia election authorities had already investigated and rejected the very allegations on which it relied.

Accountability is a critical . It is the glue that holds the justice system together and the very foundation of the rule of law. It is the pathway to affordability and to all of the rights that we hold dear.

items.title: I spent two years defending these Mississippi ballots
items.author: 1axbxsdl4pgemalky98w4g6g34ie632aghi2eb@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Lawyers like to joke that they went into law to avoid math. But my career has been marked by certain unforgettable numbers.

There is 218, the number of seats a party needs to control the U.S. House. And there’s 60, the number of votes it takes to break a Senate filibuster.

There is 428, Harry Reid’s margin of victory after his 1998 recount. And there’s 312, Al Franken’s margin over Norm Coleman after months of recounts and litigation following the 2008 election.

Today, a new number was burned into my memory: 67. That is how many absentee ballots Hinds County, Mississippi, received, processed and counted in the five business days after Election Day.

To be clear, these voters, like thousands of others across the state, did everything right. They filled out and mailed their absentee ballots by Election Day. Through no fault of their own, slow mail service meant county officials did not receive them until afterward.

In Hinds County, these ballots were reviewed and processed, and as a result, Scott Colom’s lead grew by a net 58 votes.

If Republicans had had their way, these ballots never would have been counted. They would all have been rejected for arriving too late, and the voters who cast them would have been disenfranchised.

I do not make this statement lightly or as a generalization. It is a statement of fact.

In January 2024, the Republican National Committee sued the state of Mississippi to invalidate its law allowing ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrive within five business days afterward.

By then, I had already litigated several cases against Republicans over this very issue. Because these ballots tend to skew Democratic, the RNC and its allies have repeatedly fought to have them discarded. Elias Law Group has fought just as hard to have them counted.

The RNC has been candid about its motive. “Late-arriving mail-in ballots that are counted for five additional days,” its lawyers wrote in the Mississippi complaint, “disproportionately break for Democrats.”

In a state where race and party are so closely correlated, they might as well have added that counting ballots cast by Black voters would hurt Republicans’ chances of winning. Hinds County itself is more than 70% Black.

When the RNC sued Mississippi, it seemed clear to me that it was hoping to find a friendly red state that would either quietly settle or, at the very least, not fight back hard. It did not count on my law firm intervening to defend the Mississippi law.

Over the two years that followed, on behalf of Vet Voice Foundation and the Mississippi Alliance for Retired Americans, my firm and I fought the RNC at every level of the federal courts. We won before a conservative federal district judge in Mississippi, only to see that victory reversed by the even more conservative 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

Along with the state, we took the case to the U.S. Supreme Court, though few thought we would succeed. But we did.

This past June, the Supreme Court ruled in our favor, 5-4, in Watson v. Republican National Committee.

Writing for the majority, Justice Amy Coney Barrett explained that “by default, responsibility for the mechanics of congressional elections belongs to States.” Those words would come to matter not only in Mississippi but in other cases nationwide.

At the time of the decision, most of the attention focused on what it would mean for the more than a dozen other states with laws similar to Mississippi’s. Few expected it to matter much in a state as Republican as Mississippi itself.

So, when I saw the numbers from Hinds County earlier today and realized what these voters had helped accomplish in the Senate race, I paused. It is not just that these voters would have been disenfranchised for no reason. It is that they would have been denied the chance to be part of history.

Over the last several years, Republicans have relied on the courts to advance their disenfranchisement schemes. The Supreme Court’s 6-3 decision in Louisiana v. Callais, gutting the Voting Rights Act, remains the most prominent example. But hardly the only one.

Republicans thought they would win Watson. As a voting rights lawyer, and as counsel in the case, I was thrilled they did not.

But today, my connection to this case grew deeper. It was no longer just an important precedent. It was a lifeline for democracy and free and fair elections in Mississippi.

Which is why another number will forever be burned into my mind: 4,669. Scott Colom’s margin of victory over Cindy Hyde-Smith to be elected to the U.S. Senate.
